Comment Text: An arc Fault Circuit Interrupter (AFCI) is a life-safety device (typically an AFCI circuit breaker or electrical outlet) designed to prevent fires by detecting unintended electrical arcs and disconnecting power to the affected branch circuit before the arc starts a fire. AFCI protection of bedroom receptacles (including light fixtures and smoke alarms)  was first required by the National Electric Code (NEC) in 1999 (USA) and 2002 (Canada). AFCI devices and AFCI protection requirements have changed over the years and requirements vary by jurisdiction, depending on which set of standards has been adopted.

Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI) are life-safety devices (typically a GFCI circuit breaker or electrical outlet) designed to protect people from electrical shock if they should accidentally become part of an electrical circuit. In most jurisdictions they have been required within 6 feet of a plumbing fixture for many years. Additional locations have been added periodically. As of 2023 the National Electric Code (NEC) required GFCI protection at the following locations:Bathrooms;Garages, accessory buildings and boat houses;Outdoors;Crawlspaces and Basements;Laundry areas;Damp or wet locations;Within 6 feet of a sink, tub, or shower, and At specific appliances: sump pumps, dishwashers, electric ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers and microwave ovens.GFCI protection may not have been required at all of these locations when the home was built and homes are not required to be updated when new requirements are enacted. Researching those requirements exceeds the scope of the General Home Inspection.

Because the home had a grid-tie photovoltaic system installed, a bi-directional electrical meter was installed. Bi-directional meters have three display screens. Because the home had a grid-tie photovoltaic system installed, a net electrical meter was installed. Net meters show the net consumption of power in the household. A net meter does not tell you how much solar electricity you pushed out to the grid, or how much regular electricity you took in from the grid. It indicates the difference between the two, or the net usage. A net meter runs backwards when the system is producing more electricity than you are using. The net meter has two displays or registers. The first register shows all 8s and simply means the meter is functioning properly. If something other than an 8 is shown, contact your electric company. The second register shows your net usage, and is what the electric company uses to determine how much you owe on your electric bill, or if you have generated a credit. If you used 100 kWh of energy but generated 60 of those with your solar system, the net meter will show 40.

The home was located in an area vulnerable to wildfires. Wildfire are uncontrolled fires which move across the land fueled by trees and vegetation. You should consider creating Defensible Space around your home by following your State Forest Service Guidelines. Defensible space is an area around a structure within which fuels and vegetation are treated, cleared or reduced to slow the spread of wildfire towards the structure. It also reduces the chance of a structure fire moving from the building to the surrounding forest. ZONE 1 is the area of maximum modification and treatment. It consists of an area of 15 feet around the structure in which all flammable vegetation is removed. This 15 foot dimension is measured from the outside edge of the home's eaves and from any attached structures, such as decks. ZONE 2 is an area of fuel reduction. It is a transitional area between Zones 1 and 3. The size of Zone 2 depends on the slope of the ground where the structure is built. Typically, the defensible space should extend at least 75 to 125 feet from the structure. Within zone 2, the continuity and arrangement of vegetation is modified. Remove stressed, diseased, dead or dying trees and shrubs. Thin and prune the remaining larger trees and shrubs. ZONE 3 is an area of traditional forest management and is of no particular size. It extends from the edge of your defensible space to your property boundaries. You should discuss the possibility of taking out a fire insurance policy with your insurance agent.

The Inspector disclaims confirmation of adequate attic ventilation year-round performance, but will comment on the apparent adequacy of the system as experienced by the inspector on the day of the inspection. Attic ventilation is not an exact science and a standard ventilation approach that works well in one type of climate zone may not work well in another. The performance of a standard attic ventilation design system can vary even with different homesite locations and conditions or weather conditions within a single climate zone.  
The typical approach is to thermally isolate the attic space from the living space by installing some type of thermal insulation on the attic floor. Heat that is radiated into the attic from sunlight shining on the roof is then removed using devices that allow natural air movement to carry hot air to the home exterior. This reduces summer cooling costs and increases comfort levels, and can help prevent roof problems that can develop during the winter such as the forming of ice dams along the roof eves. Natural air movement is introduced by providing air intake vents low in the attic space and exhaust vents high in the attic space.  Thermal buoyancy (the tendency of hot air to rise) causes cool air to flow into the attic to replace hot air flowing out the exhaust vents. Conditions that block ventilation devices, or systems and devices that are poorly designed or installed can reduce the system performance.

A common type of defect is voids in the concrete wall which are very difficult to detect. Another potential problem is sealing the ICF wall against moisture intrusion. This is typically done on the outside of the wall that had been backfilled at the time of the inspection and was not visible. The solar thermal system used "evacuated tube" collectors to absorb heat from the sun for use in heating home hot water.  
HOW IT WORKS The collectors mounted on the roof contain tubes. Each tube holds a heat pipe containing a fluid that turns to vapor as the tube warms. Hot vapor rises to the top of the tube, transferring its heat to a circulating fluid that in turn transfers its heat to an insulated hot water storage tank. The circulating fluid is moved through pipes by pumps which are turned on and off by an electronic controller.

The solar thermal system used "flat plate" collectors to absorb heat from the sun for use in heating home hot water.  
HOW IT WORKS 
The collectors mounted on the roof contain tubes through which a fluid circulates.  The circulating fluid is heated by the sun as it flows through tubes in the collector. The hot fluid eventually transfers its heat to an insulated hot water storage tank.  The circulating fluid is moved through pipes by pumps which are turned on and off by an electronic controller.

The home had a single-stage evaporative cooler (also called a "swamp cooler") mounted in a window.
In low-humidity areas, evaporating water into the air provides a natural and energy-efficient means of cooling. Evaporative coolers, also called swamp coolers, rely on this principal, cooling outdoor air by passing it over water-saturated pads, causing the water to evaporate into it. The 15 degrees - 40 degrees F-cooler air is then directed into the home, and pushes warmer air out through the windows.
When operating an evaporative cooler, windows are opened part way to allow warm indoor air to escape as it is replaced by cooled air. Unlike  air conditioning systems that recirculate the same air, evaporative coolers provide a steady stream of fresh air into the house.
Evaporative coolers cost about half as much to install as  air conditioners and use about one-quarter as much energy. However, they require more frequent maintenance than conventional air-conditioners and they're more suitable for areas with low humidity.
Evaporative coolers require maintenance. Here are some of the items which should be checked at the beginning of each cooling season:
- Blower assembly and motor bearings need lubrication. 
- Fan belts should have the proper tension. Belt movement should be approximately 1 inch maximum. 
- The water level should be a little below the top of the tray, with the top of the overflow pipe sticking out of the water. If the water is not at the proper level the float arm may need adjustment. 
- The water tray should be free of debris. 
- Cooler pads should be in good condition.  
- Water lines should be disconnected and blown free for the winter in cold climates.

The home contained a 2-stage evaporative cooler (also called a "swamp cooler").
Indirect Evaporative Cooling (closed circuit) is similar to direct evaporative cooling, but uses some type of heat exchanger. The cooled moist air never comes in direct contact with the conditioned environment. 
Traditional, single-stage evaporative coolers use only a fraction of the energy of conventional air-conditioning systems. Unfortunately, except for in very dry climates, they may increase humidity to a level that makes occupants uncomfortable. Two-stage (indirect) evaporative coolers do not produce humidity levels as high as that produced by traditional single-stage evaporative coolers.
The difference between a conventional evaporative cooler and an indirect evaporative cooler is that the indirect evaporative cooler cools the air in two operations before it's blown into the home to avoid adding moisture to the air. Although both operations use water for cooling, only the first operation adds moisture to supply air. 
According to manufacturers, the difference is cool air with a relative humidity between 50 and 70 percent, depending on the climate, compared to a traditional system that produces about 80 percent relative humidity air.

The home had a whole-house fan installed. Whole house fans are typically large fans with diameters in the 24 to 30-inch range. They are usually installed in the ceiling of the top floor of a home, often above a stairway. They are designed to pull cool air into the home through open lower floor windows and exhaust hot air to the home exterior through attic ventilation devices such as roof, soffit, gable or ridge vents. While whole-house fans can be effective at removing heat from a home at a relatively low cost compared to other types of cooling equipment, although they can be somewhat noisy. During the heating season, the opening in the ceiling should be sealed with an insulated cover to reduce heat loss.  IMPORTANT: While the whole-house fan is in use, it is important that windows should be partially opened to avoid de-pressurizing the home, a condition which can pull toxic exhaust gases from combustion appliances into indoor air.

Combustion appliances like furnaces, water heaters and boilers sometimes produce levels of carbon monoxide high enough to activate the alarm of the carbon monoxide detector when the system is first activated. Typically, carbon monoxide levels quickly drop to safe levels. To avoid nuisance alarms, and to protect sleeping areas, carbon monoxide detectors should be moved to appropriate locations.

No carbon monoxide detectors were installed. Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless, tasteless, toxic gas that is a product of the combustion process. Heating appliances such as gas furnaces, boilers, and wall/floor heaters can introduce dangerously high levels of carbon monoxide onto the indoor air if combustion components need adjustment. Carbon monoxide detectors are inexpensive, easy to install, and available at most hardware and home improvement stores. They should be installed as necessary to protect sleeping areas.

Comment Text: The refrigerator motor vibrated excessively at start-up, indicating a need for service.

The refrigerator cooling compartment control was at the coldest setting but the interior compartment temperature was significantly higher than the maximum recommended temperature of 40 deg. F. (4.4 C).
The refrigerator was inoperable. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified contractor to provide advice on the best course of action.
Rodent feces was visible in some kitchen cabinets. Action should be taken to eradicate rodents, cabinet interiors should be cleaned and disinfected as necessary, and points of entry sealed off.
The kitchen sink had cosmetic damage that will not affect its functionality.
A water filter was installed on the kitchen sink faucet. You should contact the manufacturer to learn about any maintenance requirements connected with its use.

Apparent moisture stains visible around at the interior of a skylight in the kitchen indicated that the skylight has leaked in the past. Leakage did not appear to be recent. The moisture meter indicated normal moisture levels at the stained areas. You should ask the seller whether this problem has been corrected.

Apparent moisture stains visible around at the interior of a skylight in the kitchen indicated recent leaking. The moisture meter indicated elevated moisture levels at the stained areas. You should consult with a qualified roofing contractor to discuss options and costs for correction.

Apparent moisture stains visible around at the interior of a skylight in the kitchen appeared to be the result of moisture from air in the living space condensing on the surface of the glass. This condition did NOT indicate loss of thermal integrity.
The interior of a skylight in the kitchen exhibited minor damage from exposure to the ultra violet rays of the sun.
The interior of a skylight in the kitchen exhibited moderate damage from exposure to the ultra violet rays of the sun.
The interior of a skylight in the kitchen exhibited severe damage from exposure to the ultra violet rays of the sun.

A switch cover plate was missing in the kitchen. This condition left energized electrical components exposed to touch, a shock/electrocution hazard. The Inspector recommends that a listed cover plate be installed.
A switch in the kitchen was scorched. This condition indicates a possible fire hazard. It should be investigated and repairs made as necessary by a qualified electrical contractor.

Switch cover plates were missing in the kitchen. This condition left energized electrical components exposed to touch, a shock/electrocution hazard. The Inspector recommends that listed cover plates be installed.

Some switches in the kitchen appeared to be inoperable. These switches may connect to exterior lights which are controlled by photo sensors and so will operate only at night. They may be improperly wired and represent a potential fire hazard or they may connect to outlets which were not tested. Switches sometimes control only the upper or lower half of an outlet. Tracing the devices controlled by all switches exceeds the scope of the general home inspection. You should take action to confirm that these switches are safe, either by asking the seller or having them traced by a qualified electrician.

The inspector was unable to determine what device is controlled by a switch in the kitchen. If the homeowner cannot provide an explanation you should have it traced by a qualified electrical contractor to ensure that safe conditions exist.
The tiled kitchen countertops exhibited minor damage.
The tiled kitchen countertops were moderately damaged (small chips/minor cracks).
The tiled kitchen countertops were severely damaged/deteriorated. You should consult with a qualified contractor to discuss options and costs for replacement.
Grout lines of the tiled kitchen countertops exhibited minor deterioration.
Grout lines of the tiled kitchen countertops were moderately deteriorated.
Grout lines of the tiled kitchen countertops were severely deteriorated. You should consult with a qualified contractor to discuss options and costs for grout repair or replacement.
Grout lines of the tiled kitchen countertops were dirty and needed maintenance.

A light installed beneath an upper cabinet did not respond to the switch. If after the bulb is replaced this light still fails to respond, a problem may exist with the switch, wiring, or fixture, and an evaluation and any necessary repairs should by made by a qualified electrical contractor.

A single plumbing trap beneath the kitchen sink served two drains located more than 30 inches apart from each other. This condition can cause siphoning that can pull all the water out of the trap, with the potential to allow sewer gas to enter the living space. Corrections should be made as necessary by a qualified contractor.

Comment Name: Under-sink: air admittance valve, less than 4" above trap arm
Comment Text: An air admittance valve beneath the kitchen sink was installed at less than the minimum 4 inches above the trap arm (horizontal drainpipe). This condition may prevent the vent from performing as designed and should be corrected by a qualified plumbing contractor.

The floor of the kitchen sink cabinet exhibited damage from moisture intrusion. The moisture meter showed no elevated levels of moisture present in the floor indicating that the source of the leak may have been corrected.

The floor of the kitchen sink cabinet had moisture damage. The moisture meter showed elevated levels of moisture present in the floor indicating recent leakage. The source of the leak should be identified and corrected by a qualified plumbing contractor to avoid further damage to the cabinet and potentially the wall/floor structure.
Hot and cold water supply connections were reversed at the kitchen sink faucet. This is a potential scalding hazard and should be corrected.

Apparent microbial growth (possible mold) was visible at damp, water-damaged areas of the kitchen under-sink cabinet. This growth should be removed as necessary. The source of moisture should be identified and corrected by a qualified plumbing contractor.

No water supply shut-offs were installed beneath the kitchen under-sink cabinet. This condition will complicate faucet repairs. Hot and cold water shut-offs should be installed by a qualified plumbing contractor.

The interior of the kitchen sink cabinet had an odor typically associated with elevated moisture levels. Although damage to the cabinet floor appeared to be moisture-related, the moisture meter showed no elevated levels of moisture present in the cabinet floor, indicating that the source of moisture may have been corrected, or may be intermittent. Further investigation may require removal of the cabinet floor, which would require the seller's permission.

The interior of the kitchen sink cabinet had an odor typically associated with elevated moisture levels. Materials beneath the kitchen sink were damp. The source of moisture should be identified and corrected. If the odor remains, deteriorated materials may need to be replaced. All work should be performed by a qualified contractor.
A water supply pipe in the kitchen under-sink cabinet was leaking. Repairs should be made immediately by a qualified plumbing contractor.
The floor of the kitchen sink cabinet was badly damaged and will need replacement. All work should be performed by a qualified contractor.

In the under-sink kitchen cabinet, leaking connections at the trap assembly should be repaired by a qualified plumbing contractor to avoid future/additional damage to the cabinet floor and possibly the wall/floor structures.

A trap in the under-sink kitchen cabinet was not approved for this purpose. Traps are designed to prevent toxic sewer gas from entering the living space. Any such traps should be replaced with approved traps by a qualified plumbing contractor.

A trap in the under-sink kitchen cabinet was of a type no longer allowed in new construction. Traps are designed to prevent sewer gas from entering the living space. An approved trap should be installed by a qualified plumbing contractor
An uncapped opening in a waste pipe in the under-sink kitchen cabinet can allow sewer gas to enter the living space. This condition should be corrected by a qualified plumbing contractor.

Comment Name: Under-sink: trap seal depth excessive (4" max.)
Comment Text: The water seal in a trap in the under-sink kitchen cabinet exceeded the manufacturer-recommended 4-inch (102 mm) maximum depth limit and may not perform adequately. Traps are designed to prevent sewer gas from entering the living space. This trap should be replaced with an approved trap by a qualified plumbing contractor.

Comment Name: Under-sink: trap seal depth inadequate (2" min.)
Comment Text: The water seal in a trap in the under-sink kitchen cabinet had less than the manufacturer-recommended 2-inch (51 mm) minimum water depth and may not perform adequately. Traps are designed to prevent sewer gas from entering the living space. This trap should be replaced with an approved trap by a qualified plumbing contractor.

No trap was installed at the drain pipe in the under-sink kitchen cabinet. Traps are designed to prevent sewer gas from entering the living space. An approved trap should be installed by a qualified plumbing contractor
To prevent cabinet damage, heavily corroded water supply pipes in the kitchen under-sink cabinet should be replaced by a qualified plumbing contractor before they develop leaks.
The upper kitchen cabinets had separated from the ceiling or soffit and should be securely re-attached by a qualified contractor.

A wall-hung light fixture did not respond to the switch. If after the bulb is replaced this light still fails to respond, a problem may exist with the switch, wiring, or fixture, and an evaluation and any necessary repairs should by made by a qualified electrical contractor.

Wall logs will move slightly with seasonal changes in humidity. The inspection of this home is designed to reflect it's visual condition at the time of the inspection only. Conditions may change to some degree seasonally, or as logs dry to moisture equilibrium content with the homesite environment (newer homes).

You may find that portions of the home exterior need to have sealant applied occasionally. Caulk from the hardware store is not durable enough and will shrink and crack. You should contact one of the following for advice on a variety of products (including sealants) they sell that are produced specifically for log homes:SashcoPermachink
Adjustable steel posts supporting floor framing were inadequately secured from lateral movement at their bottoms. This condition should be corrected as necessary by a qualified contractor.

Comment Name: Adjustable steel posts, no footing apparent
Comment Text: Adjustable steel posts supporting floor framing did not appear to bear on a foundation footing but appeared to bear on the concrete slab only. Adjustable steel posts are required to bear on a foundation footing that provides more support than a slab alone. Confirmation of proper conditions would require the services of a qualified contractor.
Adjustable steel posts supporting floor framing were inadequately secured at their tops. This condition should be corrected as necessary by a qualified contractor.

Adjustable steel posts used as permanent structural floor support were heavily corroded to a degree that may affect their ability to adequately support the loads imposed on them. They should be evaluated- and a recommendation made- by a qualified foundation contractor.

Comment Name: Adjustable steel posts: out of plumb
Comment Text: Adjustable steel posts supporting floor framing were significantly out of plumb. An evaluation should be performed and recommendation made by a qualified foundation contractor.

Comment Name: Adjustable steel posts: temporary used as permanent
Comment Text: Adjustable steel posts used as permanent structural floor support were designed as temporary supports only. This condition is potentially hazardous. Temporary posts should be replaced with posts designed for permanent support by a qualified contractor.

The Inspector was unable to confirm the presence of backer rod behind the chinking. Confirmation must be made during the chinking application process. Once application is complete, backer rod is hidden from view.

Floor structure support beams had inadequate bearing. Modern safety standards recommend that beams have a minimum of 3 inches (76 mm) bearing at their ends where they rest upon masonry or concrete. An evaluation and work as necessary should be performed by a qualified contractor.

A wood floor structure support beam had significant decay where it rested in a pocket in a masonry wall. This condition will reduce the beam's ability to support the structural loads it was designed to carry. You should consult with a qualified contractor to discuss the best course of action.

In the basement, a wood girder had inadequate surrounding air space where it rested in a pocket in a masonry wall. This condition can slow the drying process if damp conditions are allowed to develop, encouraging decay. Advanced decay will reduce the girder's ability to support the structural loads it was designed to carry. You should be diligent in making efforts to control moisture levels that may affect this condition.

Comment Name: Beam pocket: improper shim, crushing visible
Comment Text: Shims supporting a girder that supported floor structure framing were of a material not designed for this application. Shims should be of a material that will not crush under the weight of the load they support. Some crushing was visible. All such shims be replaced with shims of a proper material.

Comment Name: Beam pocket: improper shim, no crushing obseerved
Comment Text: Shims supporting a girder that supported floor structure framing were of a material not designed for this application. Shims should be of a material that will not crush under the weight of the load they support. No crushing was visible.

Joints between exterior wall log courses appeared to have been sealed using an inappropriate sealant. This product exhibited widespread failure, and may require removal and reapplication of all chinking at significant cost. This condition should be evaluated by a contractor experienced in log home restoration.

Chinking installed on the exterior of log walls did not appear to have been applied by those with adequate knowledge or skills. For a more accurate opinion on the severity of this condition, the chinking should be evaluated by a contractor experienced in log home restoration. Costs for chinking work can be significant.

Concrete masonry units (CMU, commonly known as concrete block) installed as supports beneath the floor structure support beams were installed in their weak orientation. This condition is improper, could result in structural failure, and should be corrected by a qualified contractor.

Although the Inspector uses techniques such as probing and visual examination in an effort to determine the presence of wood decay in the logs of log structures, these techniques are not technically exhaustive and will not reveal the presence of wood decay hidden in inaccessible places, such as log cores and/or the intersections of log walls. For this reason, locating or identifying wood decay which is not readily visible or decay of logs in inaccessible areas of log homes lies beyond the scope of the General Home Inspection or Log Home Inspection. Wood decay weakens logs and can compromise their ability to support structural loads.

Door and window opening logs were not keyed during construction. "Keying" would have meant slotting log ends at the sides of the openings and inserting a rigid spline to support wall logs which were cut to create the openings. Failure to key the openings results in loss of vertical log alignment at openings. This loss of alignment may worsen, resulting in increased amounts of air leakage and heat gain or loss around these openings. If bowing becomes extreme enough, it may result in structural damage to the door opening and damage to the doors or interference with their operation. You should consult with a contractor familiar with log home construction in order to discuss the necessity, options and costs for correction.

Door opening logs were not keyed during construction. "Keying" would have meant slotting log ends at the sides of the openings and inserting a rigid spline to support wall logs which were cut to create the openings. Failure to key the openings results in loss of vertical log alignment at openings. This loss of alignment may worsen, resulting in increased amounts of air leakage and heat gain or loss around these openings. If bowing becomes extreme enough, it may result in structural damage to the door opening and damage to the doors or interference with their operation. You should consult with a contractor familiar with log home construction in order to discuss the necessity, options and costs for correction.

Comment Name: Electrical: no allowance for settling, newer home, no damage
Comment Text: Electrical conduit appeared to have been installed in a manner that will not accommodate settling of log walls. This condition may result in damage to conduit and the electrical wiring it contains as log walls settle, and is a potential fire hazard. Because the home is relatively new, settling of log walls may continue. The inspector saw no damage attributable to this condition at the time of the inspection. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified contractor familiar with the requirements unique to log homes to determine the options and costs for any necessary corrections.

Comment Name: Electrical: no electrical allowance for settling, newer home, damage
Comment Text: Electrical conduit appeared to have been installed in a manner that will not accommodate settling of log walls. Some conduit showed bowing or distortion that appeared to be a result of this condition.  Not all electrical components were visible. As log walls settle, this condition may result in increasing damage to electrical components and is a potential fire hazard. Because the home is relatively new, settling of log walls may continue. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified contractor familiar with the requirements unique to log homes to provide advice on the best course of action.

Comment Name: Electrical: no electrical allowance for settling, stable home, no damage
Comment Text: Electrical conduit appeared to have been installed in a manner that will not accommodate settling of log walls. The inspector saw no damage attributable to this condition. Because of the age of the home, any log shrinkage should be complete, the log walls relatively stable, and future settling would typically be only minor and long-term. The potential for electrical problems to develop from lack of settling accommodation is very low.

Engineered floor joists appeared to be inadequately connected. Engineered lumber has specific connection and fastening requirements and failure to adhere to these requirements may affect the structural integrity of the home. An evaluation and any necessary corrections should be performed by a qualified contractor.

Engineered lumber used in the floor structure was left exposed to weather at various places around the home exterior where the floor structure rested upon the foundation. Engineered lumber is not designed for permanent exposure to weather. These areas should be permanently protected from moisture intrusion. All work should be performed by a qualified contractor.

Comment Name: Evidence of a fire, structure OK
Comment Text: The floor framing had charring indicating that the floor structure had experienced a fire. The floor structure appeared to be sound at the time of the inspection.

Floor framing had charring indicating that the floor structure had experienced a fire. The affected framing should be evaluated by a qualified contractor to determine the extent of the damage and to discuss options and costs for any necessary repairs.

Floor framing had charring indicating that the floor structure had experienced a fire. The Inspector recommends that before the expiration of your Inspection Objection Deadline you have this condition evaluated by a structural engineer to determine whether structural components weakened by fire retain sufficient residual strength. Depending on the engineers recommendation you may need to consult with a qualified contractor to discuss options and costs for any necessary repairs
The Inspector was unable to identify the type of sealant used as chinking or confirm its compatibility with the finish coating material. It appeared to be performing adequately.

Comment Name: Finish coating condition: deterioration, minor to moderate, varied with exposure to weather
Comment Text: The exterior finish coating protecting wall logs exhibited minor to moderate deterioration depending on exposure to weather and sunlight. Maintaining an intact finish coating will extend the lifespan of the wall logs. Application of a new finish coating can be expensive. An evaluation should be performed by a contractor experienced in log home restoration to provide an estimate for work as necessary. New finish coatings must be chemically compatible with underlaying existing coatings or chinking.

Comment Name: Finish coating condition: deterioration, moderate to severe, varied with exposure to weather
Comment Text: The exterior finish coating protecting wall logs exhibited moderate to severe deterioration depending on exposure to weather and sunlight. Maintaining an intact finish coating will extend the lifespan of the wall logs. Application of a new finish coating can be expensive. An evaluation should be performed by a contractor experienced in log home restoration to provide an estimate for work as necessary. New finish coatings must be chemically compatible with underlaying existing coatings or chinking.

The finish coating protecting wall log exteriors was in poor condition and did not provide adequate protection of the logs. Logs that are inadequately protected from sun and moisture will suffer damage/deterioration from ultra-violet (UV) radiation in sunlight and from moisture, including decay and freeze damage. Application of a new finish coating can be expensive. An evaluation should be performed by a contractor experienced in log home restoration to provide an estimate for work as necessary. New finish coatings must be chemically compatible with underlaying existing coatings or chinking.

Comment Text: Where joists overlapped, they were supported by a central support beam that was supported by posts that rested on concrete pads.

Comment Text: Floor joists rested on top of and were supported by beams which rested in pockets in the poured foundation walls.

Comment Text: Floor joists rested on top of and were supported by poured concrete foundation walls.

Comment Text: No flashing protected the area where the floor structure rested on the foundation wall. Comment Text: No flashing protected the area where the floor structure rested on the foundation wall, this joint was protected by a sealant only. Sealant will eventually dry, shrink, and crack. You should consult with a qualified contractor to discuss the best course of action.
Localized raised areas (humps) in the floor structure appeared to be due to poor workmanship. You should consult with a contractor to discuss options and costs for correction.

Comment Name: Floor structure: insulation, installed backing down, elevated moisture levels
Comment Text: Floor structure insulation in the unheated crawlspace was installed with the backing toward the cold side. Thermal insulation should always be installed with the backing toward the warm side. Elevated moisture levels across floor framing indicated that this condition has caused excessive amounts of condensation to develop. If it becomes severe enough, framing decay or mold growth can develop. This condition has the potential for severe, expensive-to-repair floor structure damage. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified contractor to provide an estimate for correction.

Comment Name: Floor structure: insulation, installed backing down, OK
Comment Text: Floor structure insulation in the unheated crawlspace was installed upside down. Thermal insulation should always be installed with the backing toward the warm side. Installing insulation with the backing toward the cold side can cause excessive amounts of condensation to develop. No problems were observed that appeared to be related to this condition.

Comment Name: Floor structure: insulation, loose, missing insulation
Comment Text: Floor structure insulation  in the unheated crawlspace was loose or missing. Insulation should be secured or replaced to help reduce heating costs and increase home comfort.

No Floor structure insulation was installed. This condition will draw heat from the living space, increasing heating costs and reducing comfort levels. You should consult with a qualified contractor to discuss options and costs for insulating the floor.

Posts that supported the floor structure had decayed bases that will eventually crush and fail. This will compromise the integrity of the floor structure and any structural load it supports and may result in serious structural damage. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified contractor to provide an estimate for work as necessary.

Posts supporting the floor assembly exhibited advanced wood decay where they rested on the footing. Decay will eventually weaken these support posts to the point at which they will no longer support the structural loads they were designed to carry and they will fail. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified contractor to provide an estimate for work as necessary.

Home floors were not level but sloped. This condition appeared to be the result of soil/foundation movement. Comment Name: Floor structure: sloping floor, older home
Comment Text: Home floors were not level but sloped toward the outside walls. This condition is not unusual in a home of this age, and in the inspector's opinion this condition is more a cosmetic concern than a structural concern. Determining the likelihood that movement will continue and this condition will worsen exceeds the scope of the General Home Inspection and would require the services of a specialist such as a qualified foundation contractor or a structural or geological engineer.

Comment Name: Floor structure: stains beneath sliding glass door, dry
Comment Text: Wood framing beneath the sliding glass door exhibited staining typical of moisture intrusion. The moisture meter measured no elevated levels of moisture indicating recent leakage. This may indicate that the source of moisture has been corrected or the source may be intermittent. If it continues, this type of moisture intrusion can lead to damage of the floor structure from wood decay. This framing should be checked during periods of heavy rain to ensure that leakage has not continued.

Comment Name: Floor structure: stains/decay beneath sliding glass door, elevated moisture levels
Comment Text: Wood framing visible in the crawlspace beneath the sliding glass door exhibited staining and decay typical of moisture intrusion. Comment Text: Wood framing visible in the crawlspace beneath the sliding glass door exhibited advanced decay. Repairs should be made as necessary by a qualified  contractor .

Comment Text: Caulking visible as squeeze-out between log courses indicated that it was applied between logs as new courses were added. Caulking will initially help limit air movement and the resulting heat gain/loss through the wall, but over time will dry and shrink, becoming less effective.

The home was of a type commonly called "Handcrafted". The exterior walls of Handcrafted homes are constructed using naturally-shaped logs which are scribed (marked) and cut in a manner which allows each log to fit tightly over the log in the course below. The skill and accuracy with which logs are scribed and cut, along with a gasket material typically installed in the groove between log courses, work together to resist heat, air, moisture and insect movement through the wall structure.

Wood decay is caused by decay fungi that require moisture levels of approximately 20% or above to be active. At moisture levels below this, fungi will be inactive and no decay will take place. Active decay fungi weaken wood by consuming material in wood cells. Exterior wall logs depend on an appropriate finish coating to prevent moisture absorption and the resulting risk of decay. If left unprotected, wood may weakened by decay to the point at which it becomes structurally unsound. Because correcting areas of advanced decay can be very costly, it is important to avoid the development of decay by performing preventative maintenance such as maintaining exterior finish coatings. Parts of a log home which hold and retain moisture will be more likely to experience decay. "Checking" is cracking that occurs naturally as logs dry and shrink. Checking on upper surfaces of logs will trap and hold rain and snowmelt, providing fungi with the moisture they need to actively deteriorate logs. Other areas vulnerable to decay are lower wall logs, exterior corners, roof corbels and window sills. Long roof overhangs are helpful in protecting the home. Soil and snow drift will hold moisture against the home and speed deterioration. Finishes and sealants are available which will help protect logs, but waterproofing logs is a mistake. Any finish or sealant applied to logs must be water vapor permeable. This means that the finish or sealant must allow water vapor to pass through while preventing water in liquid form from being absorbed into the log. Waterproofing logs may trap moisture in the log core, possibly causing it to decay from the inside out. In this situation, the decay may be hidden and not discovered until too late. Whole homes have been lost in this manner.

Comment Name: About conventional storage tank water heaters
Comment Text: Storage tanks water heaters are the most common type of water heater. They consist of an insulated tank in which water is heated and stored until needed. When a hot water valve is opening somewhere in the home, hot water is pulled from a pipe at the top of the water heater. To prevent overheating resulting in the development of excessive pressure in the tank (with the potential for high-energy explosion) a temperature/pressure relief (TPR) valve is installed that is designed to open if either exceeds a preset level. Natural-gas water heaters typically use less energy and cost less to run (by about half) than electric water heaters, although gas models cost more at the time of purchase.

A roof-mounted solar collector absorbs the suns heat and transfers it to an antifreeze-like fluid in a closed-loop system that runs to- and circulates through- coils inside the water tank, where heat transfer takes place. High-quality systems deliver stellar savings in summer, making them attractive for warm, sunny regions. But savings suffer on cold and cloudy days. Most models employ a backup system that activates automatically when needed. Even with federal and local rebates, payback times can be long.

Heat pump (hybrid) water heaters capture heat from the air and transfer it to the water. They use about 60 percent less energy than standard electric water heaters. And while they cost more than electric-only models, installation is similar and payback time is short. But they don't work well in very cold spaces and need to be placed in an area that stays between about 40 F and 90 F. Because the heat pump is on top of the storage tank, they require as much as 7 feet of clearance from floor to ceiling, up to 1,000 cubic feet of uncooled space to capture enough heat from the air, and a nearby drain to discharge the condensate.

Tankless water heaters heat water directly without the use of a storage tank. When a hot water tap is opened, cold water enters the heater and is heated by either a gas burner or an electric element. Tankless water heaters deliver a constant supply of hot water, on demand. You don't need to wait for water in a storage tank to be heated. The downside is that the supply of hot water may not be able to keep up with demand. Typically, tankless water heaters provide hot water at a rate of 2–5 gallons (7.6–15.2 liters) per minute. Gas-fired tankless water heaters produce higher flow rates than electric ones. Sometimes, however, even the largest, gas-fired model cannot supply enough hot water for simultaneous, multiple uses in large households. Sometimes multiple heaters are installed to alleviate this problem.

The wood shingle roof had interlayment installed. Interlayment is an asphalt-saturated felt membrane installed between courses of wood shingles to help prevent leakage. Installation of interlayment is a defective condition when used with wood shingles. It will slow the drying process, encourage decay, and shorten the expected long-term service life of the wood shingle roof. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified roofing contractor to provide advice on the best course of action.

The slate roof was installed with interlaid felt. This is typically done in order to spread slate tiles further apart and save on weight, material, and installation costs. The lifespan of felt underlayment is typically much shorter than that of slate tile. Once the underlayment has deteriorated, the chance of roof leakage will increase significantly. Correction may require extensive/expensive work. An evaluation should be performed by a qualified roofing contractor experienced in slate roofs. Not all roofing contractors will be qualified. You should be diligent in checking references.

The slate roof was installed with a synthetic interlayment. This is typically done in order to spread slate tiles further apart and reduce roof  weight, material and installation costs. The lifespan of the slate roof may depend to some degree on the lifespan of the interlayment material.

Black felt interlayment was visible between shakes, indicating that installers were not qualified. A properly installed wood shake roof will have no felt visible once installation is complete. Felt is not designed to withstand direct exposure to weather and this condition may reduce the service life of the shake roof. Consult with a qualified roofing contractor to determine the necessity, options, and costs for correction.

The wood shake roof had no interlayment installed. Interlayment is an asphalt-saturated felt membrane installed between shake courses to help prevent leakage. Lack of interlayment is a defective condition in the climate zone in which the home is located. This condition increases the chances of roof leakage. Consult with a qualified roofing contractor to determine the necessity, options, and costs for correction.

Wood shakes on this roof were installed without interlayment. According to the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau, this is acceptable when straight-split or taper-split shakes are installed in snow-free areas at weather exposures of less than 1/3 the total shake length. This roof complies.

Wood shakes had underlayment instead of interlayment installed. This condition may shorten the lifespan of the roof by slowing the drying of wet shakes. Correction may require extensive work. Comment Text: Lapped metal panels without lap sealant were installed on a roof with a slope with less than 3 inches of vertical rise in 12 inches of horizontal run (3:12). Slate was installed on a roof with a slope of less than 4&12. At slopes less than 4&12 slate is considered to be decorative only, and a waterproof membrane should be installed beneath the slate. Without waterproof underlayment, the potential for roof leakage on a roof with a slope less than 4&12 is significantly greater than when slate is installed on slopes 4:12 or steeper. Correction may require removal and replacement of all slate roofing. Consult with a contractor experienced in slate roof restoration and repair to discuss options and costs for correction.

The roof was covered with roll roofing. Roll roofing is composed of a fiberglass mat saturated with asphalt onto one side of which, granules are bonded. The purpose of the granules is to reflect the ultra violet (UV) rays of the sun which would quickly damage the felt/fiberglass backing if it were left unprotected.  
Roll roofing comes in rolls approximately 3 feet tall and is installed on the roof in overlapping horizontal courses, shingle fashion.  The amount of overlap depends upon the degree of roof slope. Roofs having less slope need greater amounts of overlap. NRCA considers mineral surface roll roofing to be a steep-slope roofing material. 
Asphalt roll roofing materials may be applied on the following slopes: 
-  on 4/12 slopes or more, if applied parallel to the rake using the exposed nail method.  
-  on 3/12 slopes or more, if applied parallel to the rake using the concealed-nail method. 
-  on 6/12 slopes or more, if applied parallel to the downslope roof edge or eaves, using the exposed nail method.  
-  on 2/12 slopes or more, if applied parallel to the downslope roof edge or eaves, using the concealed-nail method.

Shingle condition indicated that the shingle warranty may not yet have expired. Confirmation would require documentation. Shingles may have one warranty, two warranties, three warranties, or no warranty at all. A warranty may transfer once with the sale of the home, or it may transfer as a limited warranty, or it may transfer fully. Time limits for notifying the shingle manufacture of the sale of the home may exist. You should read the terms of any warranty carefully to determine whether any action is necessary by you, or by the seller, for the warranty to remain in effect.
The length of the warranty is not an accurate reflection of the actual long-term expected service life or of the remaining service life of the shingles. Manufacturer's warranties are a sales tool.

Warranties, especially longer ones, often prorate to zero at the end of the warranty period. This would mean that, if, in the 30th year of its life, a roof with shingles warranted for 40 years failed, the warranty may cover only 25% of the roof's total replacement cost, since the shingles were already 75% of the way through their warranty period.  Even less than that time period might be covered, if that's how the warranty was written. A lifetime warranty does not mean that the roof will be covered for replacement cost as long as the homeowner lives in or owns the home.

Patches in the TPO roof membrane indicate that repairs have been made. If the TPO membrane has a valid warranty it may require that any repairs comply with the manufacturer's specifications for the warranty to remain in effect. You should ask the seller about a warranty.

Failure to provide timely notification to the roof membrane manufacturer of membrane damage or leakage, of changes in roof-mounted equipment, or failure to perform inspections, repairs, or routine maintenance according on a schedule that complies with the manufacturer’s warranty terms may result in voiding of the roof membrane warranty. You should read the warranty terms carefully to ensure that any applicable warranty remains in effect.

The manufacturer's warranty is limited to shingle defects that are caused by the manufacturing process. It covers defects that cause shingles to fail before the term of the warranty has expired. This is called premature failure. Manufacturers' warranties are not negotiable, so a homeowner can't negotiate with a contractor or salesperson for a better manufacturer's warranty.
Shingles may be warranted for 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, although the 50-year warranty may also be called a lifetime warranty.
When a home is sold, the manufacturer's warranty may not transfer to the new owner at all, or it may transfer one time, or it may transfer with limited coverage, or it may transfer fully. It all depends on how the warranty was written.

Some manufacturers' warranties cover installation errors, but they require installation by manufacturer-certified installers using the manufacturers' products exclusively, from the underlayment on up.

The second type of warranty is the contractors warranty. It covers proper installation methods and workmanship. The terms of a contractors warranty may be negotiable, so they also vary. Jurisdictional requirements may influence the terms.  Jurisdictional requirements include those instituted by a city, county, state or provincial government.
Although manufacturers' and contractors' warranties are technically separate, improper installation or damage caused by workers may shorten the service life of a roof, in which case the manufacturer would deny the claim and refer the homeowner to the contractor.
There often is no single cause of shingle failure. The forces that have the greatest effect on shingles are different in different climate zones, and will be further influenced by many other conditions. If a leak occurs within the first few years of roofing installation, the leak is probably installation-related. If a new roof lasts for a few years but fails prematurely, the cause is usually manufacturing-related, although an older roof may also fail prematurely because of poor design or maintenance.  
The real cause of failure is not always obvious and may involve a combination of factors.
You should ask about any roof warranties that may transfer with the sale of the home and read the terms carefully. If the roof is not covered by a warranty, you may want to purchase an insurance policy that will pay for roof damage.
Put simply, the terms of manufacturers' warranties can vary widely. If the seller claims that a warranty is a selling point, you should review the warranty terms carefully.

Manufacturers' warranties may cover only the cost of new shingles, or a portion of their costs, but not the cost of labor for installation, especially further along in the warranty period. Labor costs for installation are affected by the roof pitch. There's typically an extra charge for steeper pitches, which may not be included in the original warranty.
Roof replacement may require removal and disposal of the existing shingles, and that may not be covered, either.

It appeared that composite slate installers may have failed to follow the manufacturer's installation instructions. With some manufacturers, failure to follow the installation instructions will void the warranty. Confirmation for this roof would require research exceeding the scope of the General Home Inspection and would require the services of a qualified roofing contractor.

The wind warranty is almost always a separate section within the overall manufacturer's warranty, and the time period covered is generally shorter than that of the overall warranty.
The average wind warranty for 20- to 40-year shingles is five years.  For 50-year shingles, it's 10 years. This is because shingles become less wind-resistant as they age.

To avoid potential damage to home materials or the development of unhealthy conditions related to mold, the source of moisture should be identified and the condition corrected. Comment Text: No gap was left between roof sheathing panels. The manufacturers recommend leaving a 1/8th-inch gap between panels to allow for moisture-related expansion. Although rare, this condition has the potential to cause bowing or buckling of roof sheathing.

Comment Name: Overframe valley jack decay, repair roof leakage
Comment Text: The overframe valley jacks exhibited advanced decay (rot) beneath the valley. This is typically the result of long-term roof leakage at the valley. This condition weakens the connection between the overframe roof and the main roof. Roofing materials at the valley were in poor condition. Repairs should be made as necessary by a qualified contractor.

Comment Text: The overframe valley jacks exhibited advanced decay (rot) beneath the valley. This is typically the result of long-term roof leakage at the valley. Consider having an evaluation performed by a qualified contractor to provide advice on the need for structural repairs.

Comment Name: Purlin bears on ceiling joists, strongback installed
Comment Text: Braces of the purlin assembly providing additional support to rafters were installed in a manner that transferred the roof load to a strongback supported at both ends, but that also rested upon ceiling joists. This condition has the potential to cause ceiling joists to sag. No joist sagging was observed, indicating that the strongback has been structurally adequate.

Comment Name: Purlin bears on sagging ceiling joists
Comment Text: Bracing of the purlin system designed to support rafters was installed in a manner that transferred the roof load to ceiling joists. Purlin braces should rest on top of a bearing wall.  This condition has caused ceiling joists to sag. Sagging will probably worsen over time unless steps are taken to correct this condition. An evaluation and any necessary work should be performed by a qualified contractor.

Comment Text: A purlin assembly installed to help support roof rafters was poorly designed and installed and had failed in areas, resulting in sagging of the roof rafters in these areas. The home had a whole-house fan installed. Whole house fans are typically large fans with diameters in the 24 to 30-inch range. They are usually installed in the ceiling of the top floor of a home, often above a stairway. They are designed to pull cool air into the home through open lower floor windows and exhaust hot air to the home exterior through attic ventilation devices such as roof, soffit, gable or ridge vents.
While whole-house fans can be effective at removing heat from a home at a relatively low cost compared to other types of cooling equipment, although they can be somewhat noisy. During the heating season, the opening in the ceiling should be sealed with an insulated cover to reduce heat loss.
While the whole-house fan is in use, it is important that windows should be partially opened to avoid de-pressurizing the home, a condition which can pull toxic exhaust gases from combustion appliances into indoor air.
